issues.description: Transitive() drops descriptor.proto only when len(files) > 0, but the slicing idiom is opaque and lacks an invariant comment
issues.detail: In ir_imports.go, Transitive() uses `i.files[:max(0, len(i.files)-1)]` to exclude an implicit trailing descriptor.proto entry. The invariant — that descriptor.proto is always the LAST element of i.files when present, and that an empty files slice means no imports at all — is nowhere stated. A literate-programming comment naming this invariant (and why it's safe to assume) belongs next to the slice. Without it, a future reader cannot tell whether `max(0, len-1)` is defending against a real edge case or papering over a bug. Decision label: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT.

issues.description: AllMembers() iteration index is now decoupled from the iterated sequence and the invariant is no longer obvious
issues.detail: Previously `i := 0; iterx.Map(f.arenas.members.Values(), ...)` made the relationship between the counter and the arena values local and readable. The new form declares `raw iter.Seq[*rawMember]`, conditionally assigns it, then iterates while incrementing `i`. The loop invariant — `i` equals the 1-based index of the current rawMember within f.arenas.members — is still correct, but a reader now has to reason across a nil-guard and a deferred assignment to see it. Either state the invariant in a comment or pull the nil case out as an early `return func(yield func(Member) bool) {}` so the happy path reads top-to-bottom. Decision label: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT.

issues.description: DescriptorProto() returns nil on zero receiver but silently returns nil on empty files too, conflating two distinct cases
issues.detail: After the nil guard, `imported, _ := slicesx.Last(i.files)` will return the zero `imported` (and thus `imported.file == nil`) when `i.files` is empty. So both `i == nil` and `i != nil && len(i.files) == 0` yield the same `nil` answer. That may be fine, but the function's contract does not state it, and the existing invariant comment in Transitive() suggests descriptor.proto is always present when there are any imports. A one-line comment stating 'returns nil iff this file has no imports recorded' would make the function readable without running it. Decision label: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT.

issues.description: Reflection-based zero test iterates methods in declaration order and only checks accessors with zero in-args; the audited surface is not stated
issues.detail: testZeroAny filters on `m.Func.Type().NumIn() != 1 || m.Func.Type().NumOut() == 0`. This excludes any accessor that takes an index (e.g. an At(i) method on a returned Indexer is exercised indirectly via Len()==0, but direct accessors taking arguments are not exercised at all). The test's coverage claim — 'getters/accessors on zero values return zero values and do not panic' — is therefore narrower than it appears. Stating the exact predicate in a comment ('we audit only nullary accessors; indexed accessors are covered transitively via Indexer.Len()==0') would make the test honest about what it proves. Decision label: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT.

issues.description: Repeated `var slice T; if f != nil { slice = ... }` pattern begs for a small helper
issues.detail: ir_file.go now contains roughly nine near-identical blocks of the form: declare a zero-valued slice, conditionally populate it from f, then pass it to seq.NewFixedSlice. The pattern is correct and the asymptotics are unchanged (O(1) per call), but the repetition obscures intent. A tiny helper like `func nilSafe[T any](f *File, get func(*File) []T) []T { if f == nil { return nil }; return get(f) }` would collapse the noise and make the nil-safety invariant explicit at one site rather than nine. Not a correctness issue; a readability one. Decision label: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT.

issues.description: Element.ValueNodeIndex sentinel choice (-1) is documented in the doc comment but the test special-cases it by name
issues.detail: The doc comment now says 'If the element is empty, this returns -1.' Good. But the test in zero_test.go hardcodes the method name `ValueNodeIndex` to expect -1. This couples the test to a method-name convention rather than a property (e.g. 'methods returning an `int` index where 0 is a valid index return -1 for the zero value'). If another such method is added later, the test will silently pass with a wrong zero value. Consider an interface or struct tag that marks 'zero-sentinel' methods, or at minimum a TODO comment naming the convention. Decision label: UNDER-AUDITED.

issues.description: Asymptotic cost of zero-guarding accessors is unchanged but allocation behavior on zero receiver should be stated
issues.detail: Each guarded accessor now creates a zero-valued local slice (`var slice []id.ID[T]`) before passing it to seq.NewFixedSlice. Go's escape analysis should keep these on the stack since they are nil slice headers, and seq.NewFixedSlice over a nil slice should produce an Indexer of length 0 without allocation. This is the right asymptotic answer (O(1), no heap). Worth a one-line comment on seq.NewFixedSlice (if not already there) confirming it tolerates nil and does not allocate — otherwise these hot-path accessors could quietly start allocating if NewFixedSlice changes. Decision label: ASYMPTOTICALLY-OK-PRACTICALLY-SLOW (potential, not confirmed).

review.summary: The diff is RIGOROUS in the sense that matters most: it identifies a real class of latent bugs (panics on zero values), adds defensive nil/IsZero guards at every relevant accessor, and lands a reflection-driven test that exercises the surface uniformly. The algorithmic content is trivial — O(1) guards, no complexity claims to audit, no data-structure choices to question — and the data structures are unchanged. My concerns are entirely literate-programming concerns. The repeated `var x T; if f != nil { x = ... }` pattern across ir_file.go is correct but noisy, and several non-obvious invariants (descriptor.proto is the last element of i.files; AllMembers' index counter; the test's coverage predicate; the ValueNodeIndex=-1 sentinel) deserve one-line comments so the code is readable without running it. No P0 issues; this is a sound improvement that should ship with light commenting polish.
